newsitem.title: CANADA: Union begins strike at General Motors Canada unit.
newsitem.headline: Union begins strike at General Motors Canada unit.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union president Buzz Hargrove said the union began a strike against U.S. General Motors Corp's Canadian subsidiary less than two hours before a strike deadline.
Hargrove said some of the union's workers went on a strike while the company was delivering a last minute economic package, which it had promised the union yesterday.
"So we are on strike," Hargrove said. "Our plants are down." He said GM's last minute economic offer was an insult to the union and a "total joke."

Hargrove said the company's economic package was crafted by executives at GM's headquarters in Detroit and that he told GM Canada's lead negotiator, Dean Munger, the union believed the talks had been sunk by the parent company.
"I told him (Munger) I thought that the document that he presented tonight was drafted by someone in Detroit that doesn't realize there is a border," he told reporters at a press briefing.
Hargrove said he expected the balance of GM Canada's 15,500 workers at its Oshawa, Ontario and Ste-Therese, Quebec operations to be on strike by midnight (0400 GMT).
Earlier this week, the union approved an escalating strike strategy in which 15,500 of its 28,000 GM members were to go on strike at midnight on Wednesday.
Other GM Canada facilities would join the strike starting on October 6 and the entire Canadian operation would be shut down by October 9.
GM Canada acknowledged the union's reaction to the economic package, saying the union was unhappy with it.

The CAW has said its C$50 million strike fund could last up to eight weeks. That could stretch to 16 weeks if the union mortgaged some properties. Hargrove has also said that the union had set a special strike dues convention for October 18 for all 210,000 CAW members.
The major unresolved issue in the talks is the contracting out of jobs to non-union suppliers, generally known as "outsourcing".
GM Canada said it planned to sell two Ontario plants and outsource work at several plants for a total cost of 5,500 CAW jobs and the union has said it is determined to resist.
